item.title: Assignment 8: Simplification, Normal Forms, and Properties of CFLs
item.description:
This assignment evaluates and deepens your understanding of Context-Free Grammar (CFG) simplification, normal forms (Chomsky and Greibach), the CYK parsing algorithm, the CFL Pumping Lemma, and closure/decision properties, synthesizing Michael Sipser (Chapter 2.1 & 2.3) and Peter Linz (Chapters 6 & 8).

Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous mathematical justification.

Question 1

If a Context-Free Grammar \(G = (V, T, S, P)\) is in Chomsky Normal Form (CNF), then for any non-empty string \(w \in L(G)\) of length \(n = |w| \ge 1\), every derivation of \(w\) in \(G\) takes exactly \(2n - 1\) steps.

item.title: Assignment 7: Turing Machines, Decidability, the Chomsky Hierarchy, and Computational Complexity
item.description:
This assignment evaluates and deepens your understanding of Turing Machines (TMs), TM variants, the Church-Turing Thesis, decidability versus recognizability, Cantor’s diagonalization, mapping reducibility, the extended Chomsky Hierarchy, and the fundamentals of computational complexity (\(P\) vs \(NP\)), synthesizing the core principles from Michael Sipser (Parts 2 & 3) and Peter Linz (Chapters 9–12, 14).

Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous mathematical justification.

item.title: Assignment 6: Pushdown Automata and Deterministic Parsing
item.description:
This assignment evaluates and deepens your understanding of Pushdown Automata (PDAs), nondeterministic versus deterministic computation, equivalence with Context-Free Grammars (CFGs), Deterministic Context-Free Languages (DCFLs), and deterministic parsing principles, synthesizing Michael Sipser (Chapters 2.2 & 2.4) and Peter Linz (Chapter 7).

Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous mathematical justification.

Question 1

In a Pushdown Automaton (PDA), acceptance by final state and acceptance by empty stack are equivalent in power for nondeterministic PDAs (NPDAs). However, for Deterministic PDAs (DPDAs) without an explicit endmarker, acceptance by empty stack recognizes a strictly smaller class of languages than acceptance by final state (specifically, prefix-free DCFLs).

item.title: Assignment 5: Context-Free Languages and Grammars
item.description:
Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous mathematical justification.

Question 1

If a context-free grammar $G$ is unambiguous, then for every string $w \in L(G)$, there exists exactly one leftmost derivation and exactly one rightmost derivation, and both derivations correspond to the same unique parse tree.

Question 2

The family of regular languages is a proper subset of context-free languages. Consequently, every right-linear grammar is context-free, but not every context-free grammar is regular.

item.title: Assignment 4: Properties of Regular Languages
item.description:
Slide Set 4 Assignment: Properties of Regular Languages

This assignment is designed to evaluate and consolidate your mastery of the closure properties of regular languages, decision algorithms (elementary questions), and the Pumping Lemma, synthesizing the rigorous theoretical frameworks of Michael Sipser (Chapter 1.4) with the constructive algorithmic proofs of Peter Linz (Chapter 4).

Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous mathematical justification.

item.title: Assignment 3: Regular Grammars
item.description:
Slide Set 3 Assignment: Regular Expressions and Regular Grammars

This assignment is designed to test and deepen your understanding of the concepts covered in Slide Set 3, synthesizing Peter Linz’s focus on regular grammars and algebraic transitions with Michael Sipser’s rigorous GNFA state-elimination methods.

Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous mathematical justification.

Question 1

The languages denoted by the regular expressions $R_1 = (a^*b^*)^*$ and $R_2 = (a \cup b)^*$ are identical.

item.title: Assignment 2: Finite Automata
item.description:
Slide Set 2 Assignment: Finite Automata (DFA, NFA, and Minimization)

This assignment is designed to test and deepen your understanding of the concepts covered in Slide Set 2, synthesizing the intuitive design patterns of Peter Linz (Chapter 2) with the mathematical rigor of Michael Sipser (Chapter 1.1–1.2).

Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous mathematical justification.

Question 1

In a Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$, the transition function $\delta$ can map a state-symbol pair to the empty set ($\emptyset$) to represent a dead-end or “trap” configuration.

item.title: Assignment 1: Prerequisites
item.description:
Slide Set 1 Assignment: Mathematical Preliminaries, Languages, and Grammars

This assignment is designed to test your understanding of the foundational mathematical preliminaries, string operations, formal languages, and basic grammars covered in Slide Set 1 (synthesizing material from Sipser Chapter 0 and Linz Chapter 1).

Section A: True or False Questions

For each question, select True or False and provide a rigorous justification grounded in the definitions.

Question 1

If $A$ is an empty set ($\emptyset$), then its power set $2^A$ is also empty ($\emptyset$).
